# My Plan for This Year

I have been working this land for 40 years, so I pretty much know what I am doing. My 10 mu is split up: about 7 mu I do wheat in winter and then maize right after harvest in summer — that is the main rotation, almost everyone here in Quzhou does it. The other 3 mu on the south end I keep for cotton. Cotton prices have not been great lately but I know cotton, I have grown it my whole life, and the soil there suits it.

My wife's brother works in the city now, so it is mostly just the two of us. I hire a hand or two at busy times, like wheat harvest and cotton picking.

---

**Wheat — 7 mu, October through June**

I sow around October 5th to 8th. Last year I used Jimai 22 and got decent results. Old Wang next door used the same and did well, so I will stick with it. Before sowing I do rotary tillage twice to get a fine seedbed.

For fertilizer: I put in about 100 kg of diammonium phosphate (DAP) and 50 kg of urea as base across the 7 mu — that is roughly 14 kg DAP and 7 kg urea per mu. Then in March at jointing I throw on another 15 kg of urea per mu as topdressing. I also mix in about 10 kg of potassium sulfate per mu at base because I read in a leaflet the dealer gave me that potassium helps with stalk strength and I had some lodging three years ago.

Irrigation: four times — once before sowing if the ground is dry, once in November for winter water to protect the roots from freeze, once at jointing in March, once at heading in early May. The well handles this fine.

Pesticides: herbicide after emergence in November, then around April I spray for aphids and powdery mildew together. Three applications total. Last year I had some rust late in the season that cost me yield, so I will watch more carefully this time.

I expect around 480 kg per mu if weather is normal.

---

**Maize — 7 mu, June through September**

Right when wheat is off, I go straight in with maize — no ploughing, just direct seeding. The neighbors all do this now and it saves two or three days of work plus money. I use a hybrid, either Zhengdan 958 or Xianyu 335, whatever the dealer has in stock.

I put all the compound fertilizer in at sowing — about 50 kg of NPK compound (15-15-15) per mu — and then topdress with 15 kg urea per mu at the big bell stage when the plant is waist high and growing fast. That is when it needs nitrogen most.

For water: I rely on the summer rains mostly. I irrigate once at sowing if the ground is too dry, and once at tasseling if we hit a dry spell. Two times usually.

Pesticide: herbicide right after sowing, then one spray for corn borer if I see damage. Two applications.

I expect 560 to 580 kg per mu.

---

**Cotton — 3.1 mu, April through October**

Cotton I start in early April, raising seedlings in a small seedbed, then transplanting in early May once the soil is warm. I use a hybrid variety with bollworm resistance — the dealer in town sells one, I have used it three years running and it is reliable.

Before transplanting I plough that field — I still plough for cotton, the roots go deep and they need loose soil. I work in about 50 kg of compound fertilizer per mu as base, plus an extra 10 kg of potassium sulfate per mu because cotton likes potassium for fiber quality. Then I topdress three times through the season with urea, about 10 to 12 kg each time.

Cotton needs more water than wheat or maize. I irrigate five times: at transplanting, bud stage, first flowering, peak boll period, and once more in August if it stays hot and dry.

Pesticide: cotton is the most work. Aphids come early, then thrips, then bollworm from July. I spray five times through the season, maybe six if bollworm pressure is heavy.

I expect about 280 kg per mu of seed cotton. Some years it is better, some years pests eat into it.

---

**Budget worry:** Cotton uses the most pesticide money and the most irrigation electricity. Maize fertilizer adds up too. My total input costs across the whole farm will probably run 8,000 to 10,000 yuan. With my son sending some money back from the city, we can manage, but I do not want to cut inputs on wheat — a bad wheat harvest is a real problem for us.
